topicDisplay: D1–D2 — Continuity and change: molecules and cells
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Helicase opens the helix; DNA polymerase builds the new strands
Using PCR and electrophoresis: DNA profiling in forensics and paternity
Translation: a ribosome turns mRNA codons into a polypeptide
What mRNA, the ribosome and tRNA each do
Why the code uses triplets, and what degenerate and universal mean
Reading an mRNA sequence with the codon table
A single base change can change a protein
A substitution may change one amino acid, or none
Insertions and deletions usually wreck the polypeptide
Mutation is random, but not evenly spread
Cytokinesis is usually equal, but not always
Mitosis keeps the genome; meiosis halves it and adds variety

Reading the phase from a diagram or micrograph

questions.q: A drug inhibits helicase but has no effect on DNA polymerase. What will happen to DNA replication in a cell treated with the drug?
options: Replication cannot begin, because the hydrogen bonds between the strands are not broken, so no template strand is exposed.
Replication continues normally, because DNA polymerase unwinds the double helix itself as it copies each strand.
New strands are made but fall off the template, because helicase forms the hydrogen bonds that hold new bases in place.
Cell division continues without replication, because the existing DNA is simply shared between the two daughter cells.
optionWhy: Helicase is needed to unwind the helix and break the hydrogen bonds between the strands. Without it the strands stay paired, no template is exposed and DNA polymerase has nothing to copy.
A student who gives the unwinding job to DNA polymerase picks this. DNA polymerase only assembles new strands on templates that helicase has already exposed.

A student who thinks an enzyme makes the base pairs picks this. Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases form spontaneously; helicase's role is to break them, and without it no strand is even started.
A student who thinks division halves the DNA picks this. Each daughter cell must receive a complete copy of the DNA, so without replication normal division cannot proceed.
questions.explain: Helicase is needed to unwind the helix and break the hydrogen bonds between the strands. Without it the strands stay paired, no template is exposed and DNA polymerase has nothing to copy.

questions.q: A DNA profile was prepared for a mother, her child and a man who may be the father. The fragment lengths (in base pairs) in each profile were: mother 100, 220, 260, 340; child 100, 150, 220, 300; man 150, 180, 300, 330. What can be concluded?
options: The man is excluded as the father, because two of his bands (180 and 330) do not appear in the child's profile.
The man cannot be excluded as the father: the child's two bands not from the mother (150 and 300) are both in his profile.
The man is excluded as the father, because the child's profile does not match his profile completely.
The man is proved to be the father, because DNA profiles are unique and two of his bands match the child's.
optionWhy: A student who expects the child to carry all of the father's bands picks this. A child inherits only half of each parent's DNA, so bands in the father that the child did not inherit are expected.

The child's bands 100 and 220 came from the mother. The remaining bands, 150 and 300, must come from the biological father, and both appear in the man's profile, so he cannot be excluded. Further markers would be used to make the conclusion more reliable.
A student who applies forensic-style complete matching to paternity picks this. Only the child's bands that are not explained by the mother need to be present in the father.
A student who treats any match as proof picks this. Sharing bands at a few markers is consistent with paternity but does not prove it; other men could share the same fragment lengths by chance.
questions.explain: The child's bands 100 and 220 came from the mother. The remaining bands, 150 and 300, must come from the biological father, and both appear in the man's profile, so he cannot be excluded. Further markers would be used to make the conclusion more reliable.

questions.q: What happens during translation?
options: A base sequence of DNA is used as a template to make a complementary mRNA molecule inside the cell nucleus.
Ribosomes convert the bases of the mRNA into amino acids, which are then joined into a chain.
The base sequence of an mRNA molecule is used to determine the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide.
Amino acids are joined into a polypeptide inside the nucleus, right beside the DNA of the gene that codes for it.
optionWhy: A student who has swapped the two terms picks this. Making mRNA on a DNA template is transcription; translation is the synthesis of a polypeptide from the mRNA.
A student who thinks amino acids are made from bases picks this. The amino acids already exist in the cytoplasm and are brought by tRNA; the mRNA only determines the order in which they are joined.
Translation is the synthesis of a polypeptide from mRNA: the base sequence of the mRNA, read as codons, is translated into the amino acid sequence of the polypeptide on a ribosome.
A student who keeps the whole process in the nucleus picks this. Translation takes place on ribosomes in the cytoplasm, after the mRNA has left the nucleus.
questions.explain: Translation is the synthesis of a polypeptide from mRNA: the base sequence of the mRNA, read as codons, is translated into the amino acid sequence of the polypeptide on a ribosome.

questions.q: A cell contains many different kinds of tRNA molecule. What is the role of a tRNA during translation?
options: It brings a specific amino acid to the ribosome and pairs its anticodon with the matching codon on the mRNA.
It binds to a codon first and then collects from the cytoplasm whichever amino acid that codon specifies.
It delivers an amino acid and remains bonded to it, becoming part of the finished polypeptide chain.
It carries the mRNA bases that the ribosome converts into the amino acids of the polypeptide.
optionWhy: Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon complementary to the codons for that amino acid, so complementary base pairing at the ribosome delivers the amino acid the codon specifies.
A student who thinks the codon tells the tRNA what to fetch picks this. The amino acid is attached to the tRNA before it reaches the ribosome; the codon selects which loaded tRNA binds.
A student who thinks tRNAs stay in the chain picks this. Once its amino acid has been joined to the polypeptide by a peptide bond, the tRNA leaves the ribosome and is reused.
A student who thinks amino acids are made from bases picks this. tRNA carries an amino acid, not bases to be converted; the mRNA bases only specify which amino acid is added.
questions.explain: Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon complementary to the codons for that amino acid, so complementary base pairing at the ribosome delivers the amino acid the codon specifies.

questions.q: The gene for human insulin has been inserted into bacteria, which then translate it into a polypeptide with the same amino acid sequence as the polypeptide made in human cells. Which feature of the genetic code makes this possible?
options: Universality: the bacterium's tRNAs assign exactly the same amino acids to the codons as human cells do.
Universality: bacteria and humans have the same genes, so the bacterium already had an insulin gene.
Degeneracy: each codon can be read as several amino acids, so the bacterium can make any protein.
Complementary pairing: bacterial tRNA anticodons pair directly with the bases of the inserted DNA.
optionWhy: The genetic code is universal: with minor exceptions, the same codons specify the same amino acids in all organisms, so the bacterium translates the human mRNA into the same amino acid sequence.
A student who takes universal to mean 'same genes' picks this. Universality is about the meaning of codons, not the genes; bacteria have no insulin gene, which is why one had to be inserted.

A student who thinks degenerate means ambiguous picks this. Each codon specifies one amino acid; the bacterium makes the human polypeptide because it reads the codons the same way, not because it can read them differently.
A student who thinks tRNA pairs with DNA picks this. The inserted gene is transcribed into mRNA first, and it is the shared meaning of the mRNA codons that makes the product identical.
questions.explain: The genetic code is universal: with minor exceptions, the same codons specify the same amino acids in all organisms, so the bacterium translates the human mRNA into the same amino acid sequence.

questions.q: An mRNA molecule has the base sequence AUGUUUGCUUAAGGC, read from the first base. The genetic code table gives: AUG methionine (start), UUU phenylalanine, GCU alanine, UAA stop, GGC glycine. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide translated from it?
options: two amino acids
four amino acids
three amino acids
fifteen amino acids
optionWhy: A student who does not count the start codon picks this. AUG codes for methionine as well as marking the start, so methionine, phenylalanine and alanine make three.
A student who reads past the stop codon to include GGC picks this. UAA ends translation, so the glycine codon after it is not translated.

The codons are AUG UUU GCU UAA GGC. AUG gives methionine, UUU phenylalanine and GCU alanine; UAA is a stop codon, so translation ends there and GGC is never translated. The polypeptide has three amino acids.
A student who thinks each base codes for one amino acid picks this. The code is a triplet code, so 15 bases form 5 codons, of which one is a stop codon and only three are translated.
questions.explain: The codons are AUG UUU GCU UAA GGC. AUG gives methionine, UUU phenylalanine and GCU alanine; UAA is a stop codon, so translation ends there and GGC is never translated. The polypeptide has three amino acids.

questions.q: Two mutations occur near the start of the coding sequence of the same gene, in different cells: in one cell a single base is substituted; in the other a single base is inserted. Which mutation is more likely to change the structure of the protein, and why?
options: Neither is likely to, because each changes only a single base and so can affect at most one amino acid.
The substitution, because a substitution is certain to change an amino acid, while an insertion adds only one.
Neither is likely to, because the ribosome recognizes each codon wherever it starts reading.
The insertion, because it shifts the reading frame so that every codon after it is read differently.
optionWhy: A student who assumes a one-base change means a one-amino-acid change picks this. An insertion shifts the reading frame and alters every subsequent codon.
A student who thinks every substitution changes an amino acid picks this. Many substitutions are silent, and an insertion does not add one amino acid but changes the reading of all that follow.
A student without a fixed reading frame picks this. The ribosome reads consecutive triplets from the start codon, so an inserted base makes it read every later triplet in the wrong frame.

Adding one base changes how all the following bases are grouped into codons, so the amino acid sequence from that point onward is altered. A substitution changes at most one amino acid and may be silent.
questions.explain: Adding one base changes how all the following bases are grouped into codons, so the amino acid sequence from that point onward is altered. A substitution changes at most one amino acid and may be silent.

questions.q: The same gene was sequenced in 1000 people. At one position 62% carry C and 38% carry T, and the two resulting codons code for the same amino acid. How should this difference be described?
options: A rare mutation causing disease in the 38% group
A frameshift mutation that affects later codons
An SNP that leaves the polypeptide unchanged
A substitution that changes one amino acid
optionWhy: A student who equates SNP with genetic disease picks this. A variant carried by 38% of people is common, not rare, and both versions code for the same amino acid, so there is no basis for calling it disease-causing.
A student who thinks a substitution shifts the reading frame picks this. One base has been replaced by another, not added or removed, so every codon stays in place.

A single base differs between individuals at one position: this is a single-nucleotide polymorphism, the result of a base substitution that has spread in the population. Because both codons specify the same amino acid, the polypeptide is unchanged.

A student who assumes every codon change alters the amino acid picks this. The stem states that both codons code for the same amino acid, which is possible because of the degeneracy of the genetic code.
questions.explain: A single base differs between individuals at one position: this is a single-nucleotide polymorphism, the result of a base substitution that has spread in the population. Because both codons specify the same amino acid, the polypeptide is unchanged.

questions.q: Two copies of a gene are mutated at the same point in the coding sequence. In copy X three consecutive bases are inserted; in copy Y one base is inserted. Which comparison is correct?
options: X keeps the reading frame so the codons after it are unchanged, but Y shifts the frame for every later codon
Both X and Y shift the reading frame, so both of the polypeptides are likely to cease to function
Both X and Y alter just one amino acid at the insertion point, leaving the rest unchanged
Y changes every amino acid, including those before the insertion, whereas X adds just one amino acid
optionWhy: Three bases is a whole codon, so in X the codons after the insertion are grouped exactly as before: the polypeptide gains one amino acid (possibly with one adjacent amino acid altered) and the rest is unchanged. One extra base in Y is not a multiple of three, so every later codon is regrouped: a frameshift that is likely to abolish function.

A student who thinks every insertion causes a frameshift picks this. The frame shifts only when the number of bases inserted is not a multiple of three, so X, with three bases inserted, keeps the frame.

A student who assumes one base change means one amino acid change picks this. It is roughly true for X, but the single extra base in Y regroups every codon after it, changing the whole of the rest of the polypeptide.

A student who thinks a frameshift alters the amino acids before the mutation as well picks this. The X clause is correct, but in Y the ribosome reads the codons before the insertion exactly as before; only the codons after it are regrouped.
questions.explain: Three bases is a whole codon, so in X the codons after the insertion are grouped exactly as before: the polypeptide gains one amino acid (possibly with one adjacent amino acid altered) and the rest is unchanged. One extra base in Y is not a multiple of three, so every later codon is regrouped: a frameshift that is likely to abolish function.

questions.q: A bacterial culture that has never been exposed to the antibiotic streptomycin is found to contain about one resistant cell per 10⁷ cells. When streptomycin is added, the resistant cells survive and the culture soon consists almost entirely of resistant cells. What do these observations show?
options: The antibiotic caused the bacteria to mutate the gene that gives resistance because they needed it in order to survive
The resistance mutation arose by chance before exposure, and the antibiotic then selected the cells carrying it
Most mutations in bacteria are beneficial, which is why the resistance spread through the culture so quickly
The resistance allele was created by recombination during reproduction rather than by mutation
optionWhy: A student who believes mutation is directed by need picks this. The resistant cells existed before the antibiotic was added, so the antibiotic cannot have caused the mutation; it only selected the cells that already carried it.

Resistant cells were already present at a low frequency in a culture that had never met the antibiotic, so the mutation must have occurred at random beforehand. Adding streptomycin did not create resistance; it killed the sensitive cells and left the resistant ones to multiply.

A student who thinks mutation is mostly helpful picks this. Resistance was present in only one cell in ten million, consistent with a rare beneficial mutation among many harmful or neutral ones; it spread because selection removed the sensitive cells.

A student who credits reproduction with making new alleles picks this. Bacteria in the culture reproduce asexually, and in any organism recombination only reshuffles existing alleles: a new allele can arise only by mutation.
questions.explain: Resistant cells were already present at a low frequency in a culture that had never met the antibiotic, so the mutation must have occurred at random beforehand. Adding streptomycin did not create resistance; it killed the sensitive cells and left the resistant ones to multiply.

questions.q: In human oogenesis, the first meiotic division produces a large secondary oocyte and a very small polar body. What does this unequal cytokinesis achieve?
options: The oocyte keeps almost all the cytoplasm and organelles for the future zygote, while both cells receive a complete haploid set of chromosomes.
The oocyte receives a larger share of the chromosomes along with the extra cytoplasm, so the polar body has fewer chromosomes to be discarded.
The polar body is the result of a failed equal division; in normal oogenesis the cytoplasm is divided equally between two egg cells of equal size.
The polar body is a fragment of cytoplasm pinched off without a nucleus, so the oocyte keeps all of the chromosomes from the division.
optionWhy: Unequal cytokinesis concentrates the cytoplasm, with its organelles and nutrient stores, in the one cell that can become an egg. Nuclear division has already shared the chromosomes equally, so the polar body has a full haploid set but almost no cytoplasm.
A student who thinks a bigger cell must hold more genetic material picks this. Meiosis I gives each product one chromosome of every pair; the inequality is only in the cytoplasm.
A student who believes cytokinesis is invariably equal picks this. Unequal division is the normal course of human oogenesis and is one of the guide's two examples of unequal cytokinesis.

A student who pictures a bud or fragment forming without nuclear division picks this. The polar body receives one of the two nuclei produced by meiosis I; it is small because it receives almost no cytoplasm.
questions.explain: Unequal cytokinesis concentrates the cytoplasm, with its organelles and nutrient stores, in the one cell that can become an egg. Nuclear division has already shared the chromosomes equally, so the polar body has a full haploid set but almost no cytoplasm.

questions.q: Nuclear division normally occurs before the cytoplasm of a cell is divided. What would result if a cell divided its cytoplasm into two without first dividing its nucleus?
options: Each daughter cell would build itself a new nucleus from the DNA and proteins present in its share of the cytoplasm.
Both daughter cells would receive a nucleus, because DNA replication has already doubled the number of chromosomes to provide two sets.
One daughter cell would be anucleate: with no chromosomes it could not transcribe genes to replace its proteins or divide again.
This could not happen, because splitting the cytoplasm is the final phase of mitosis and so must follow the division of the nucleus.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a nucleus can be assembled like any other organelle picks this. Chromosomes exist only as copies of previous chromosomes, so a nucleus can arise only by division of an existing nucleus.

A student who thinks replication produces two sets of separate chromosomes picks this. Replication produces two chromatids in each chromosome inside one nucleus; only nuclear division can separate them into two nuclei.
Nuclear division is needed before cell division to avoid the production of anucleate cells. A cell without a nucleus has no genome, so it can make no new mRNA and cannot divide.
A student who treats cytokinesis as a phase of mitosis picks this. Cytokinesis is a separate process from nuclear division, which is why the guide emphasizes that nuclear division is needed first.
questions.explain: Nuclear division is needed before cell division to avoid the production of anucleate cells. A cell without a nucleus has no genome, so it can make no new mRNA and cannot divide.

questions.q: In both mitosis and meiosis, chromosomes are moved to the poles of the cell during anaphase. What causes this movement?
options: The spindle microtubules contract in the same way as muscle fibres, pulling the chromosomes towards the poles.
The separated chromatids repel one another and so drift apart to opposite ends of the cell without any attachment.
Microtubule motor proteins move the chromosomes along spindle microtubules, which shorten as the chromosomes travel.
A ring of actin and myosin at each pole contracts, dragging the chromosomes attached to it away from the equator.
optionWhy: A student who takes 'the fibres pull' literally picks this. Microtubules cannot contract; they shorten by losing subunits, and the movement is produced by motor proteins.
A student who has seen anaphase drawn without a spindle picks this. Chromatids do not move on their own; each is attached at its centromere to microtubules and moved by motor proteins.
Chromosome movement uses microtubules and microtubule motors. Motor proteins at the centromere move the chromosome along the microtubule towards the pole, and the microtubule shortens as it does so.

A student who merges the contractile ring with the spindle picks this. Actin and myosin form the ring that pinches an animal cell in cytokinesis; chromosomes are moved by microtubules and their motors.
questions.explain: Chromosome movement uses microtubules and microtubule motors. Motor proteins at the centromere move the chromosome along the microtubule towards the pole, and the microtubule shortens as it does so.

questions.q: A student counted 100 cells in a micrograph of a growing root tip. 85 cells had an intact nucleus with no visible chromosomes; 6 had condensed chromosomes scattered through the cell; 3 had chromosomes aligned across the equator; 4 had two groups of chromatids moving apart; 2 had two groups of chromosomes at the poles with nuclear envelopes forming. Which conclusion is correct?
options: All 100 cells are in mitosis, because the 85 with an intact nucleus and no visible chromosomes are in prophase.
Nine of the cells are in metaphase, because scattered and aligned condensed chromosomes both lie in the middle of the cell.
About 15% of the cells are in mitosis, and prophase is the most frequent phase among the dividing cells.
The tissue has stopped dividing, because far fewer than half of the cells show any phase of mitosis.
optionWhy: A student who takes interphase to be a stage of mitosis picks this. An intact nucleus with no distinct chromosomes is the appearance of interphase; only the 15 cells with condensed chromosomes are in mitosis.

A student who identifies metaphase by position rather than alignment picks this. Only the 3 cells with chromosomes aligned across the equator are in metaphase; the 6 with scattered chromosomes are in prophase.

The 85 cells with an intact nucleus are in interphase. The other 15 are in mitosis: 6 prophase, 3 metaphase, 4 anaphase and 2 telophase, so 15% of the cells are dividing and prophase is the commonest phase.
A student who expects mitosis to occupy most of the cycle picks this. Interphase is much the longest part of the cell cycle, so 15% of cells in mitosis is typical of an actively growing root tip.
questions.explain: The 85 cells with an intact nucleus are in interphase. The other 15 are in mitosis: 6 prophase, 3 metaphase, 4 anaphase and 2 telophase, so 15% of the cells are dividing and prophase is the commonest phase.

questions.q: Why is meiosis needed in a sexual life cycle?
options: Gametes could be produced by mitosis instead, because when two diploid gametes fuse the zygote they form is diploid like its parents.
Fertilization combines the chromosomes of two gametes, so the number must be halved beforehand to keep it constant across generations.
Each gamete must carry only half of the parent's genes, so that the offspring gets one half from each parent and no gene is duplicated.
Mitosis doubles the chromosome number each time a body cell divides, so meiosis is needed to bring the number back down again.
optionWhy: A student who does not track the chromosomes through fertilization picks this. Two diploid gametes would give a zygote with four sets, and the number would double in every generation.

Fusion of two gametes adds their chromosome sets together. Halving the number in meiosis means that fertilization restores the diploid number instead of doubling it, so the number stays constant from one generation to the next.
A student who thinks haploid means half the genes picks this. Every haploid gamete carries a full set of genes; the offspring inherits two complete sets, one from each parent.
A student who thinks mitosis doubles the chromosome number picks this. Mitosis maintains the number; it is fertilization that would double it, and meiosis compensates for fertilization.
questions.explain: Fusion of two gametes adds their chromosome sets together. Halving the number in meiosis means that fertilization restores the diploid number instead of doubling it, so the number stays constant from one generation to the next.

questions.q: A species has a diploid number of 8. Ignoring crossing over, how many different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes can random orientation of bivalents produce in its gametes?
options: 16, because each of the 4 bivalents can be oriented in 2 ways, independently of the others
8, because each of the 4 bivalents contributes 2 possible orientations to the total
256, because each of the 8 chromosomes can be oriented in 2 ways, independently of the others
4, because a gamete receives one chromosome from each of the 4 bivalents, giving 4 combinations
optionWhy: There are 4 bivalents (2n = 8, so n = 4). Each can be oriented with its maternal or its paternal chromosome facing a given pole, and the orientations are independent, so the number of combinations is 2⁴ = 16.
A student who adds the possibilities (2 + 2 + 2 + 2) or multiplies 2 × 4 picks this. Independent orientations multiply, giving 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16.
A student who uses the diploid number instead of the number of bivalents picks this. Chromosomes orient as pairs, so the exponent is the number of bivalents, 4, not 8: 2⁴, not 2⁸.
A student who counts the bivalents instead of multiplying their orientations picks this. Each of the 4 bivalents has 2 orientations, and independent orientations multiply: 2⁴ = 16.
questions.explain: There are 4 bivalents (2n = 8, so n = 4). Each can be oriented with its maternal or its paternal chromosome facing a given pole, and the orientations are independent, so the number of combinations is 2⁴ = 16.

questions.q: A student writes: "Glucose and sodium chloride both dissolve in water because water molecules form hydrogen bonds with them." How should this claim be evaluated?
options: Correct for both: hydrogen bonds are the attraction that holds every kind of dissolved particle in solution, whether it is a molecule or an ion.
Correct for glucose, whose hydroxyl groups form hydrogen bonds with water, but not for sodium chloride, whose ions are attracted to water's partial charges.
Incorrect for both: glucose dissociates into ions when it dissolves, and ions are held in solution by attraction to the partial charges on water, not by hydrogen bonds.
Incorrect for both: water dissolves each of these solutes by reacting with it and breaking its molecules or ions apart into smaller particles.
optionWhy: A student who treats hydrogen bonding as the explanation for all solvation picks this. Ions do not form hydrogen bonds; they are held by the attraction between their full charge and the partial charges of polar water molecules.

Glucose is a polar molecule with –OH groups that hydrogen-bond to water, so the claim is right for it. Sodium chloride dissolves because Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are attracted to the oppositely charged ends of polar water molecules, which is a different kind of attraction.

A student who believes only charged particles can dissolve picks this. Glucose molecules stay intact in solution; their polar hydroxyl groups form hydrogen bonds with water, so the claim is right for glucose.

A student who regards dissolving as a chemical reaction picks this. Solvation is physical: glucose molecules and sodium and chloride ions are surrounded by water molecules but are not broken down or changed.
questions.explain: Glucose is a polar molecule with –OH groups that hydrogen-bond to water, so the claim is right for it. Sodium chloride dissolves because Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are attracted to the oppositely charged ends of polar water molecules, which is a different kind of attraction.

questions.q: The cytoplasm of a red blood cell has a solute concentration equivalent to 0.9% sodium chloride. A red blood cell is placed in a 3% sodium chloride solution. What is the net movement across its membrane, and what happens to the cell?
options: Water moves into the cell and it swells, because water moves from the more concentrated solution to the less concentrated cytoplasm.
Water moves into the cell and it swells, because the 3% solution is hypotonic to the cytoplasm of the cell.
Sodium chloride moves into the cell until the solute concentrations on the two sides are equal, and the cell's volume is unchanged.
Water moves out of the cell, because the solution is hypertonic to the cytoplasm, so the cell shrinks and becomes crenated.
optionWhy: A student who moves water down the solution's concentration gradient picks this. Water moves from the lower solute concentration (the cytoplasm) to the higher solute concentration (the 3% solution), so it leaves the cell and the cell shrinks.
A student who has swapped hypo- and hyper- picks this. The 3% solution has the higher solute concentration, so it is hypertonic to the cytoplasm; water moves out of the cell and it shrinks.

A student who expects the solute to equalise the concentrations picks this. The cell membrane is partially permeable: the net movement that reduces the difference is water leaving the cell, which therefore shrinks.

The 3% solution has a higher solute concentration than the 0.9%-equivalent cytoplasm, so it is hypertonic to the cell. Net movement of water by osmosis is out of the cell into the hypertonic solution; the cell, which has no wall, shrinks and its membrane develops the crinkled outline called crenation.
questions.explain: The 3% solution has a higher solute concentration than the 0.9%-equivalent cytoplasm, so it is hypertonic to the cell. Net movement of water by osmosis is out of the cell into the hypertonic solution; the cell, which has no wall, shrinks and its membrane develops the crinkled outline called crenation.

questions.q: Paramecium is a unicellular organism that lives in fresh water. Its contractile vacuole repeatedly fills with water and then expels it from the cell. Why is this necessary?
options: The cytoplasm is hypertonic to fresh water, so water continually enters by osmosis and must be expelled to prevent swelling and bursting.
The vacuole stores the water the cell absorbs, keeping a reserve that the cell can draw on when the pond water becomes scarce.
The vacuole takes in water to replace the water the cell loses by osmosis to the fresh water, which is more dilute than the cytoplasm.
The vacuole is the pump by which the cell moves water in by osmosis, using energy whenever the cytoplasm needs more water.
optionWhy: Fresh water has a much lower solute concentration than the cytoplasm, so water enters the cell by osmosis all the time. Paramecium has no cell wall, and the contractile vacuole removes the water so that the cell does not swell and burst.
A student who associates vacuoles with storage picks this. The contractile vacuole expels water from the cell; its job is removal of excess water, not storage.

A student who moves water from the more concentrated side to the less concentrated side picks this. Water moves into the more concentrated cytoplasm, so the cell gains water and the vacuole has to remove it.
A student who thinks the cell controls osmosis actively picks this. Osmosis is passive and brings water in unasked; the energy used by the contractile vacuole goes into pushing that water out.
questions.explain: Fresh water has a much lower solute concentration than the cytoplasm, so water enters the cell by osmosis all the time. Paramecium has no cell wall, and the contractile vacuole removes the water so that the cell does not swell and burst.

questions.q: A plant cell is placed in pure water. What happens to it?
options: Water enters by osmosis and the cell swells until it bursts, like an animal cell in pure water.
Solutes leave the cell into the pure water until the cell sap is as dilute as the water outside.
The cell pumps water in, using energy, until it is full and then it switches the pumping off.
Water enters by osmosis and the cell becomes turgid, its wall resisting further expansion.
optionWhy: A student who transfers the fate of a red blood cell to a plant cell picks this. The cellulose wall resists expansion, so pressure builds up inside and net entry of water stops before the cell can burst.
A student who expects the solute to equalise the concentrations picks this. The membrane is partially permeable; it is water that moves, entering the cell.

A student who believes the cell drives osmosis actively picks this. Osmosis is passive: water enters down the gradient, and it is the pressure from the wall, not a decision by the cell, that stops net uptake.
Pure water is hypotonic to the cell sap, so water enters by osmosis. The cell wall resists expansion, turgor pressure develops, and net uptake of water stops when the cell is turgid.
questions.explain: Pure water is hypotonic to the cell sap, so water enters by osmosis. The cell wall resists expansion, turgor pressure develops, and net uptake of water stops when the cell is turgid.
